methods.params: Not shown as raw JSON-RPC. Each SDK's tool handler signature is the closest analogue to the eventual request shape: Python `async def get_alerts(state: str) -> str` (kwargs = tool arguments, docstring Args: block = per-arg description); TypeScript handler `async ({ state }) => {...}` fed by a Zod `inputSchema`; Java `@Tool`/`@ToolParam` annotated method params; Kotlin handler receives `request.arguments` as a `JsonObject` looked up by key; C# `[McpServerTool]` static method params (with `[Description]` attributes) plus a DI-injected `HttpClient`; Ruby `self.call(state:)` keyword args per `input_schema`; Rust `Parameters(MCPAlertRequest { state }): Parameters<MCPAlertRequest>` deserialized via `schemars::JsonSchema`; Go `getForecast(ctx, req *mcp.CallToolRequest, input ForecastInput)` with `input` decoded from JSON per Go struct tags.
methods.result: Every language ultimately returns/produces a text content block. TypeScript, Kotlin, Ruby, and Go samples construct the CallToolResult shape explicitly: `{ content: [ { type: "text", text: "..." } ] }` (TS), `CallToolResult(content = listOf(TextContent(...)))` (Kotlin), `MCP::Tool::Response.new([{ type: "text", text: ... }])` (Ruby), `&mcp.CallToolResult{Content: []mcp.Content{&mcp.TextContent{Text: ...}}}` (Go, 3-tuple return `(*mcp.CallToolResult, any, error)`). Python and Java and Rust and C# tools instead just `return` a plain string/Task<string>, i.e. those SDKs auto-wrap a scalar return value into the text-content result — the file never states the exact wrapping rule, it only shows the effect by omission.

requirements.text: Python STDIO servers must never write to stdout (e.g. via `print()`), because doing so corrupts the JSON-RPC message stream and breaks the server.
requirements.cite: pages/docs__2026-07-28__develop__build-server.md, Python tab, 'Logging in MCP Servers', lines 44-48

requirements.text: Python STDIO servers should use the standard `logging` module (which writes to stderr) instead of `print()`, with one logger per module via `logging.getLogger(__name__)`.
requirements.cite: same file, Python tab, 'Best Practices', lines 52-55, 60-68

requirements.text: HTTP-based servers (any language) may log to stdout freely, since stdout logging does not interfere with HTTP responses.
requirements.cite: same file, repeated verbatim in every language tab's 'Logging in MCP Servers' subsection, e.g. lines 50-51 (Python), 351 (TS), 806 (Java), 1099 (Kotlin), 1470 (C#), 1724 (Ruby), 2029 (Rust), 2448 (Go)

requirements.text: TypeScript STDIO servers must never call `console.log()`, since it writes to stdout by default and corrupts JSON-RPC messages.
TypeScript STDIO servers should use `console.error()` (stderr) or a stderr/file-based logging library.
Java STDIO servers must never use `System.out.println()`/`System.out.print()`.

Java STDIO servers should use `Host.CreateEmptyApplicationBuilder` semantics equivalent (for C#) or a stderr/file logging library (Java/Kotlin/Ruby/Rust/Go) to avoid stray console output; C# specifically must use `CreateEmptyApplicationBuilder` rather than `CreateDefaultBuilder` for STDIO transport so the host framework itself does not print startup banners to stdout.
requirements.cite: same file, C# tab, Note under 'Building your server', lines 1550-1552

requirements.text: Kotlin STDIO servers must never use `println()`.
C# STDIO servers must never use `Console.WriteLine()`/`Console.Write()`.
Ruby STDIO servers must never use `puts` or `print`.
Rust STDIO servers must never use `println!()`/`print!()`.
Go STDIO servers must never use `fmt.Println()`/`fmt.Printf()`.

wire_details: No JSON-RPC request/response payloads, no HTTP headers (no Mcp-Session-Id, no MCP-Protocol-Version, no Origin), no numeric error codes, and no MIME-type constants appear anywhere in this file. This tutorial operates entirely at the SDK-ergonomics layer (decorators/annotations/builders) and stdio process launch, never at the wire layer.

The only 'constant' string literals that recur across all 8 language tabs are the two tool names used by the running example: `get_alerts` and `get_forecast` (Java/C# use PascalCase `GetAlerts`/`GetWeatherForecastByLocation`/`GetForecast` for the method name but the underlying tool identifiers registered are still effectively these two concepts).

Claude Desktop config key is `mcpServers` (object), each entry keyed by an arbitrary server name (e.g. `"weather"`) with fields `command` (string), `args` (string array), and optionally `cwd` (string, shown only in the Ruby example to set the working directory for `bundle exec ruby weather.rb`).

Config file path is OS-dependent: `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` (macOS), `~/.config/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` (Linux), `%AppData%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json` (Windows) — stated identically in every language tab's 'Testing your server with Claude for Desktop' section.

Claude Desktop log locations (macOS/Linux only, Windows not given): `~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp*.log` (macOS), `~/.config/Claude/logs/mcp*.log` (Linux); general connection log is `mcp.log`, per-server stderr capture is `mcp-server-SERVERNAME.log`.

NWS API constants used identically across all language samples (not MCP constants, but load-bearing for behavioral parity across the comparative table): base URL `https://api.weather.gov`, `Accept: application/geo+json` request header, and a `User-Agent` header whose exact string differs slightly per language (`weather-app/1.0` in Python/TS/Ruby/Rust; `WeatherApiClient/1.0 (your@email.com)` in Java; `WeatherApiClient/1.0` in Kotlin; `weather-tool/1.0` via `ProductInfoHeaderValue` in C#).

Version floors stated in this file: Python SDK `mcp[cli]` — 'Python MCP SDK 2.0.0 or higher', Python 3.10+; Node.js 20+ for TypeScript; Java 17 + Spring Boot 3.3.x for the Java/Spring-AI sample; JDK 11+ and Kotlin SDK `0.9.0` (`io.modelcontextprotocol:kotlin-sdk`), Ktor `3.2.3`; .NET 8 SDK + NuGet package `ModelContextProtocol` installed with `--prerelease`; Ruby 2.7+ with gem `mcp`; Rust 1.70+ with crate `rmcp = "0.3"` (features `server, macros, transport-io`); Go 1.24+ with module `github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/mcp`.
sdk_implications: A PowerShell SDK's cmdlet surface should mirror the 'decorator vs explicit builder' split seen here: Python (`@mcp.tool()` decorator on a plain async function, docstring Args: block becomes per-parameter description, type hints become the JSON Schema) and Java/C# (attribute-based: `@Tool`/`[McpServerTool]` + `[Description]`/`@ToolParam` on ordinary methods, auto-discovered via `MethodToolCallbackProvider`/`WithToolsFromAssembly()` reflection) are the 'low ceremony' end. TypeScript (`server.registerTool(name, { description, inputSchema: zod-schema }, handler)`), Kotlin (`server.addTool(name, description, inputSchema = ToolSchema(...), handler)`), Ruby (class-based `MCP::Tool` subclass with `tool_name`/`description`/`input_schema` DSL + `self.call`), Rust (`#[tool_router]`/`#[tool(description=...)]` proc macros over an impl block, with `Parameters<T: JsonSchema>` extraction), and Go (freestanding `func(ctx, req, input T) (*Result, any, error)` + `mcp.AddTool(server, &mcp.Tool{Name, Description}, fn)`, schema derived from Go struct tags `json:`/`jsonschema:`) are all 'explicit registration' patterns requiring a name+description+schema triple passed to a registration call. PowerShell has no decorator/attribute-on-function primitive as clean as Python's, so the natural analogue is the Go/TypeScript/Kotlin pattern: a `Register-McpTool -Name -Description -InputSchema <hashtable|scriptblock> -ScriptBlock` cmdlet, since PowerShell functions can carry `[Parameter()]`/comment-based help metadata similar to C#'s attributes — an `Register-McpTool` cmdlet that introspects a function's `[CmdletBinding()]`/param block (analogous to C#'s `[McpServerTool]` + `[Description]` reflection route) is the closest fit to the 'low ceremony' end.

None of the 8 samples show manual JSON-RPC framing, confirming that a PowerShell SDK should hide the transport entirely behind a `Start-McpServer -Transport Stdio|Http` cmdlet, matching every language's single terminal call: Python `mcp.run(transport="stdio")`, TS `await server.connect(new StdioServerTransport())`, Kotlin `server.createSession(transport)` + manual `Job`/`onClose` wait loop, C# `builder.Services.AddMcpServer().WithStdioServerTransport()...; await app.RunAsync()`, Ruby `MCP::Server::Transports::StdioTransport.new(server); transport.open`, Rust `Weather::new().serve(transport).await?; service.waiting().await?`, Go `server.Run(context.Background(), &mcp.StdioTransport{})`. A PowerShell `Start-McpServer` should likewise block the pipeline/thread until the transport closes, and must guarantee (per the MUST NOT logging rules above) that the harness disables PowerShell's default stdout write-host path when running under `-Transport Stdio` — this is a concrete, checkable SDK requirement: `Write-Host`/unredirected `Write-Output` on the host stream must be forbidden or auto-redirected to stderr in STDIO mode.

The Go sample's 3-tuple handler return `(*mcp.CallToolResult, any, error)` is the only SDK here that separates 'structured/typed result', 'raw result object', and 'error' as distinct return channels — a PowerShell equivalent could map `error`/exception to native PowerShell terminating-error semantics (`$PSCmdlet.ThrowTerminatingError`) while letting the scriptblock's normal output become the content array, closest in spirit to Python's 'return a string, let the SDK wrap it' auto-wrapping behavior.

Every SDK's Claude-Desktop config entry is transport-agnostic JSON (`command` + `args` [+ `cwd`]) launching a native OS process; a PowerShell-authored server is just another `command: pwsh, args: [-File, /path/to/server.ps1]` (or a published `.exe`/module entry point) — no PowerShell-specific config schema is implied or required beyond what every other language already uses.

Because this file never demonstrates resources, prompts, elicitation, sampling, or HTTP transport, the PowerShell SDK plan CANNOT rely on this file alone to design `Register-McpResource`/`Register-McpPrompt`/elicitation cmdlets or `Start-McpServer -Transport Http` — those must be planned from the server-concepts, transport, and elicitation spec pages (not read in this task) plus schema.ts/schema.json.

Version-floor conventions across ecosystems (Python 3.10+, Node 20+, Java 17+/Boot 3.3+, JDK 11+, .NET 8+, Ruby 2.7+, Rust 1.70+, Go 1.24+) suggest a PowerShell SDK should likewise pin and document a minimum PowerShell version (7.x for cross-platform parity, since the container/target has 'no pwsh' currently) and a minimum SDK package version once published to the gallery, consistent with every other SDK's practice of stating an explicit floor at the top of its quickstart.

summary: This page is a hands-on tutorial ('Build an MCP server'), not the normative protocol spec: it walks through building an identical stdio-only weather MCP server (two tools: get_alerts, get_forecast) in eight language SDKs — Python (`mcp[cli]`, `@mcp.tool()` decorator on `MCPServer`), TypeScript (`@modelcontextprotocol/server`, `McpServer.registerTool(name, {description, inputSchema: zod}, handler)`, `StdioServerTransport`), Java/Spring AI (`@Tool`/`@ToolParam` annotations, `MethodToolCallbackProvider`, Spring Boot auto-config, STDIO or `STREAMABLE` protocol property), Kotlin (`kotlin-sdk` 0.9.0, `Server`/`ServerCapabilities(tools=Tools(listChanged=true))`, `server.addTool(name, description, inputSchema=ToolSchema(...))`), C# (`ModelContextProtocol` NuGet prerelease, `AddMcpServer().WithStdioServerTransport().WithToolsFromAssembly()`, `[McpServerToolType]`/`[McpServerTool]` attributes), Ruby (`mcp` gem, `MCP::Tool` subclass DSL with `tool_name`/`description`/`input_schema`), Rust (`rmcp` 0.3 crate, `#[tool_router]`/`#[tool(description=...)]` macros, `schemars::JsonSchema` request structs, `ServerHandler`), and Go (`go-sdk/mcp`, `mcp.AddTool(server, &mcp.Tool{...}, handlerFn)` with JSON/jsonschema struct tags). It gives, per language: STDIO logging must-not/should rules (never write to stdout — corrupts JSON-RPC; HTTP servers may log to stdout freely), version floors, project scaffolding commands, and a `claude_desktop_config.json` `mcpServers` entry (command/args[/cwd]) plus OS-specific config/log paths and a restart-fully-quit warning. It explicitly does NOT cover resources, prompts, elicitation, sampling, or HTTP/Streamable-HTTP server hosting — those primitives are only named in the intro or a single unelaborated Java WebFlux mention. No JSON-RPC payloads, headers, error codes, or MIME constants appear.
